cse-2021-1-cs-41.approach: Use the standard DFS-tree characterisation of articulation points and look for small counterexamples for the other claims.

steps.title: The root (A, B)
steps.body: An undirected DFS has no cross edges, so different subtrees of the root are joined only through the root. Root is a cut vertex **iff** it has ≥ 2 children. A path $a-b-c$ explored from $b$ gives a root with 2 children that is a cut vertex, so (A) is false and (B) is true.

steps.title: Leaves (C)
steps.body: Deleting a leaf of $T$ leaves the rest of $T$ intact and spanning the other vertices, so the graph stays connected. A leaf is never an articulation point: (C) false.

steps.title: Ancestor/descendant paths (D)
steps.body: Let $u$ have two child subtrees: subtree 1 has a back edge to $u$'s parent $x$, subtree 2 does not (so $u$ is a cut vertex). For $y$ in subtree 1, the path $x \to y$ via the back edge avoids $u$. (D) is false.

Removing a leaf keeps the remaining DFS tree connected.

cse-2021-1-cs-44.approach: After a reboot the server has no state for the old connection: anything the client sends is answered with RST, nothing is sent spontaneously, and the port is free to be bound again.

steps.title: Client that only waits (A)
steps.body: The rebooted server knows nothing of the connection and sends nothing. Without keepalive, a client that is only reading never sends a segment, so it can wait forever. (A) possible.

steps.title: Server side (B, C, D)
steps.body:
- (B) After reboot the server application can bind and listen on port P again — possible.
- (C) A segment for a connection the host does not know is answered with RST — possible.
- (D) FIN is sent only by an endpoint closing a connection it knows about; the rebooted host has no such connection, so no FIN.

optionAnalysis.reason: No keepalive and no data from the client → no segment ever reveals the dead connection.
The old socket died with the crash; listening on P again is normal.
TCP replies RST to a segment that does not belong to any existing connection.
FIN requires an orderly close of a known connection; the server has lost that state.

pitfalls: Assuming the server "closes" the old connection with FIN after reboot.

cse-2021-1-cs-45.approach: Fragment payloads must be multiples of 8 bytes and fit MTU − 20; only the first fragment carries the TCP header, and fragments are never retransmitted by routers.
cse-2021-1-cs-45.given:
| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| IP datagram from P | 1400 + 20 = 1420 B |
| MTU R→Q | 820 B |

steps.title: Fragment at R
steps.body: Max data per fragment $= 820 - 20 = 800$ (a multiple of 8). $1400 = 800 + 600$, so two fragments: $800 + 20 = 820$ B and $600 + 20 = 620$ B. (A) true.

steps.title: Loss of a fragment
steps.body: Routers do not buffer or retransmit fragments, so (B) is false. Q cannot reassemble the datagram and discards it; TCP at P times out and retransmits the whole 1400-byte segment (with a new IP datagram). (C) true.

steps.title: Ports
steps.body: The TCP header (with ports) is in the first 20 bytes of the payload, i.e. in fragment 1 only. (D) false.

optionAnalysis.reason: 800 + 600 data bytes; second datagram 600 + 20 = 620 B.
IP routers keep no copies of forwarded fragments.
Only TCP at P recovers losses, by resending the whole segment.
The TCP header is in the first fragment (offset 0).

pitfalls: Forgetting the 20-byte IP header when computing the 1420-byte datagram and its 800-byte split.

cse-2021-1-cs-46.approach: S = 5 lets at most two threads (2 units each) be inside at once, but a thread can be stuck holding one unit; check each claimed outcome with an explicit schedule.

steps.title: Deadlock (D)
steps.body: All five threads execute the first `wait(S)`: S drops 5 → 0. Each now blocks on its second `wait(S)` and nobody can signal. Deadlock of all threads — possible.

steps.title: counter = 5 (A)
steps.body: Run threads one after another: each does two waits, `counter++`, two signals. Final value 5 — possible.

steps.title: counter = 1 (B)
steps.body: Thread T1 enters (S = 3), reads counter = 0 and is pre-empted. T2…T5 each enter one at a time (S = 3 → 1 → 3), incrementing counter to 4. T1 resumes and writes 0 + 1 = 1. Final value 1 — possible.

steps.title: counter = 0 (C)
steps.body: Every `counter++` writes (value read) + 1 ≥ 1, and if all threads complete, at least one write happens last. The final value is ≥ 1, so 0 is impossible.

optionAnalysis.reason: Serial execution gives 5.
One thread's stale read of 0 overwriting the other four increments gives 1.
The last write is always some read value + 1 ≥ 1.
All five first waits succeed, all second waits block.

pitfalls: Assuming S = 5 serialises the increment — it allows two threads at once, so updates can be lost.

steps.title: Language
steps.body: $q_0 \to q_1$ pushes #. In $q_1$ each $a$ pushes A ($n$ times). In $q_2$ each $b$ pops an A ($m \le n$). The move to accepting $q_3$ needs A on top, i.e. $m < n$. Input must be fully read, so $L = \{a^n b^m \mid 0 \le m < n\}$.
